prompt: A junior engineer's PR has one severe security bug and four minor style issues. What's the most calibrated way to communicate this in review?
choices: Mark everything as blocking so nothing slips through
Tag the security issue as blocking with an explanation of the risk, and group the style issues as non-blocking nits
Only mention the security issue and silently fix the style issues yourself
Reject the PR without comments and ask them to find the issues themselves

prompt: Why does explaining the 'why' behind a review comment matter more for a junior engineer than for a peer reviewer?
choices: Juniors are less capable of following instructions
It makes the review take longer, which signals thoroughness
A peer can often infer the underlying principle from a terse comment; a junior often can't yet, so the lesson won't transfer to their next PR without it
It is required by most engineering style guides

prompt: In driver/navigator pairing, what is the navigator primarily responsible for?
choices: Typing the actual code changes
Watching for bugs, edge cases, and whether the overall design still makes sense, one level above the immediate line being written
Writing the commit message at the end of the session
Running the test suite after each change

prompt: A team wants to apply the same repetitive rename across 40 files with no logic changes. Is pairing a good fit for this task?
choices: Yes, pairing catches mistakes on every kind of change
No — this is mechanical work better handled with a script or by splitting the file list, since a navigator adds little value narrating boilerplate
Yes, but only if the driver is junior
No, because pairing should only be used for onboarding

prompt: In TDD ping-pong pairing, what forces the driver/navigator roles to swap?
choices: A timer that goes off every hour
Each person alternates writing a failing test and then making it pass, so the role swaps every cycle
The manager assigns roles at the start of each day
Roles never swap in ping-pong pairing

prompt: What is the purpose of the 'Alternatives considered' section in an RFC?
choices: To pad the document so it looks more thorough
To document options that were rejected and why, so the reasoning is on record and doesn't get relitigated later
To list every technology the author has ever used
It's optional and rarely included in real RFCs

prompt: In the worked webhook-delivery RFC, why was a phased rollout (shadow mode, then 5% of tenants, then ramp to 100%) proposed instead of enabling the new system for all tenants at once?
choices: Phased rollouts are required by company policy in all cases
It lets the team observe real delivery latency and dead-letter rates on a small blast radius before committing all tenants to the new path
It's slower, which looks more careful to reviewers
Feature flags only support percentage-based rollouts, never full cutover

prompt: A reviewer wants a junior's PR to also add pagination, even though the PR's actual scope is a single bugfix and pagination isn't urgent yet. What's the calibrated move?
choices: Block the PR until pagination is added, since more thoroughness is always better
Raise it as a non-blocking question or suggestion, and consider filing a follow-up ticket instead of expanding the PR's scope
Say nothing, since junior PRs shouldn't receive scope suggestions
Add the pagination code yourself without commenting
